stages.name: Iberian interior
stages.desc: Native Iberian, Celtic and other peoples beyond the colonial trade

stages.name: Tartessian heartland
stages.desc: The orientalizing chiefdoms of the lower Guadalquivir and Guadiana

stages.name: Mining zones
stages.desc: Silver, copper and lead districts that fed the eastern trade

stages.name: Phoenician colonies
stages.desc: Harbour towns founded by Tyre and, later, led by Carthage

stages.name: Greek trading sphere
stages.desc: Coasts drawn into the trade of Phocaean Greeks from Massalia and Emporion

states.name: Navarre
timeline: Urnfield farmers along the Ebro and the Pyrenean valleys

states.name: Gipuzkoa
timeline: Communities of the Basque coast and valleys

states.name: Huesca
timeline: Pyrenean herders and Urnfield villages

states.name: Lleida
timeline: Urnfield villages of the Segre valley

states.name: Girona
timeline: Urnfield villages of the Empordà plain
Phocaean Greeks found Emporion (Empúries) on the Gulf of Roses

states.name: Badajoz
timeline: Communities of the middle Guadiana, land of the warrior stelae
The Medellín necropolis: the middle Guadiana joins the Tartessian orbit
Palace-sanctuaries such as Cancho Roano flourish after the valley's crisis

states.name: Cádiz
timeline: Tyrian merchants settle the islands of Gadir; a temple to Melqart rises on the southern island
A walled Phoenician town grows at Doña Blanca on the mainland opposite Gadir
Gadir comes through the crisis and enters Carthage's sphere

states.name: Ourense
timeline: Hillforts and tin-bearing valleys of the Atlantic north-west

states.name: Cáceres
timeline: Pastoral communities of the Tagus, land of the warrior stelae
The Aliseda treasure: Tartessian gold reaches the Tagus

states.name: Salamanca

states.name: Zamora
timeline: Farming communities of the Duero, soon of the Soto culture

states.name: Pontevedra
timeline: Coastal hillforts of the Rías Baixas, linked to Atlantic seaways

states.name: Huelva
timeline: Rio Tinto and Tharsis: silver and copper mines worked with Phoenician partners at Onoba (Huelva)
The princes buried at La Joya with chariots and bronze jugs grow rich on the trade
Silver output at Rio Tinto falls sharply
Huelva's emporium shrinks; the Tartessian aristocracy is gone

states.name: Barcelona
timeline: Late Bronze Age villages of the Catalan coast, ancestors of the Laietani
Greek wares from Emporion reach the Laietanian coast

states.name: Tarragona
timeline: Villages of the lower Ebro, later visited by Phoenician traders

states.name: Castellón
timeline: Late Bronze Age villages of the northern Valencian coast

states.name: Valencia
timeline: Late Bronze Age villages of the Valencian plain

states.name: Alicante
timeline: Native villages of the Segura and Vinalopó, trading at Peña Negra
La Fonteta, a Phoenician port, is founded at the mouth of the Segura
La Fonteta is abandoned; trade passes to native Iberian towns

states.name: Murcia
timeline: Settlements of the Segura valley and its southeastern hills

states.name: Almería
timeline: Native villages of the dry southeast
Abdera (Adra) is founded at the mouth of the river Adra

states.name: Granada
timeline: Native villages of the Granada coast and its mountains
Sexi (Almuñécar) is founded; its nobles are buried with Egyptian alabaster urns

states.name: Málaga
timeline: Native villages behind the Málaga coast
Phoenicians settle Morro de Mezquitilla and Cerro del Villar at river mouths
Toscanos is abandoned; Malaka becomes the coast's main town

states.name: Seville
timeline: Late Bronze Age towns around the great estuary of the lower Guadalquivir
The sanctuary of El Carambolo overlooks the estuary; Phoenicians worship at Caura (Coria)
The valley at its height: Herodotus' king Arganthonios is said to begin his long reign
Rich burials and sanctuaries vanish; the Turdetani of later writers inherit the valley

states.name: A Coruña

states.name: Lugo
timeline: Hillforts of the Atlantic Late Bronze Age, ancestors of the Castro culture

states.name: Asturias
timeline: Hillfort communities of the Cantabrian mountains

states.name: Cantabria
timeline: Pastoral communities of the Cantabrian coast

states.name: Biscay
timeline: Communities of the Basque coast and valleys

states.name: Balearic Islands
timeline: Talaiotic communities of Mallorca and Menorca; Ibiza almost empty
Phoenicians found Ebusus on Ibiza (the date given by Diodorus)

states.name: Zaragoza
timeline: Urnfield villages of the middle Ebro valley

states.name: La Rioja
timeline: Urnfield farmers of the upper Ebro

states.name: Araba / Álava
timeline: Farming villages of the upper Ebro basin

states.name: Albacete

states.name: Teruel

states.name: Cuenca

states.name: Toledo

states.name: León

states.name: Soria

states.name: Burgos
timeline: Farming villages of the upper Duero

states.name: Ávila
timeline: Cogotas culture herders of the central sierras

states.name: Palencia
timeline: Soto culture villages of the northern Meseta

states.name: Ciudad Real
timeline: Villages of La Mancha below the Sierra Morena

states.name: Córdoba
timeline: Bronze Age hill towns of the middle Guadalquivir and the Sierra Morena
Córdoba and the middle valley join the Tartessian world
The orientalizing elite disappears from the middle valley

timeline: Upland villages of the eastern Meseta

states.name: Jaén
timeline: Bronze Age settlements of the upper Guadalquivir
Cástulo grows rich beside the lead and silver of the Linares district

states.name: Community of Madrid

events.title: Gadir founded
events.text: Tyrian merchants settle the low islands at the mouth of the Bay of Cádiz and call the place Gadir, 'the walled place'.

events.title: Traders at Onoba
events.text: Phoenician pottery, weights and tools beneath modern Huelva show trade with the locals since about 900 BC.

events.title: Temple of Melqart
events.text: On the southern island of Gadir rises the temple of Melqart, Tyre's god, with its two bronze pillars.

events.title: Morro de Mezquitilla
events.text: Phoenicians settle a headland at the mouth of the Algarrobo and work iron there.

events.title: Cerro del Villar
events.text: A Phoenician harbour town grows on an island at the mouth of the Guadalhorce.

events.title: Rio Tinto mines
events.text: A mining village on Cerro Salomón smelts silver from the red hills, with Phoenician methods.

events.title: Doña Blanca
events.text: A walled town with Phoenician houses rises on the mainland shore opposite Gadir.

events.title: El Carambolo
events.text: A sanctuary to Astarte and Baal stands on a hill above the Guadalquivir estuary, near today's Seville.

events.title: Toscanos
events.text: Phoenicians found a trading post at the mouth of the Vélez, with warehouses and fine houses.

events.title: Sexi
events.text: The Phoenician town of Sexi is founded at Almuñécar.

events.title: La Fonteta
events.text: A Phoenician port is founded at the mouth of the Segura, trading with native Peña Negra.

events.title: Caura
events.text: Phoenicians build a sanctuary at Caura, today Coria del Río, on the estuary of the Guadalquivir.

events.title: Abdera
events.text: The Phoenician town of Abdera is founded at Adra.

events.title: Laurita necropolis
events.text: Sexi's nobles are buried in rock-cut tombs with Egyptian alabaster urns.

events.title: Carmona's lords
events.text: Carmona, on its ridge above the valley, becomes a rich Tartessian town.

events.title: Córdoba
events.text: The settlement on the Colina de los Quemados joins the Tartessian trade in copper and silver.

events.title: La Joya
events.text: Huelva's nobles are buried with chariots, bronze jugs and ivory caskets.

events.title: Ebusus
events.text: Phoenicians found Ebusus on Ibiza, the date given by the Greek historian Diodorus.

events.title: Medellín
events.text: A Tartessian-style necropolis grows at Medellín on the Guadiana.

events.title: Aliseda treasure
events.text: A woman is buried near the Tagus with a gold diadem, belt and jewels in eastern style.

events.title: Cástulo
events.text: Cástulo grows rich beside the lead and silver of the Linares district.

events.title: Colaeus of Samos
events.text: Blown past the Pillars of Hercules, a Greek captain reaches Tartessos and returns rich, says Herodotus.

events.title: Arganthonios
events.text: A Tartessian king begins a reign that Herodotus says lasted eighty years.

events.title: Tartessian writing
events.text: Stelae in the southwestern script, the oldest native writing in Iberia, are carved; one is found at Villamanrique.

events.title: Greeks at Huelva
events.text: Huelva receives more Greek pottery than anywhere else in the western Mediterranean.

events.title: Phocaean friends
events.text: Arganthonios welcomes Phocaean Greeks and offers them silver to wall their city, says Herodotus.

events.title: Mainake?
events.text: Greek writers place a Phocaean colony, Mainake, on this coast; archaeologists have never found it.

events.title: Malaka
events.text: Malaka, today's Málaga, grows into the leading Phoenician town of the coast.

events.title: Emporion
events.text: Phocaean Greeks from Massalia found Emporion, 'the market', on the Gulf of Roses.

events.title: Tyre submits
events.text: After a thirteen-year siege, Tyre submits to Babylon; Gadir and the western colonies are left on their own.

events.title: Toscanos abandoned
events.text: The central settlement at Toscanos is deserted; its people move across the river.

events.title: A long reign ends
events.text: Arganthonios dies; the Greeks remember him as the richest of kings.

events.title: La Fonteta abandoned
events.text: The Phoenician port at the mouth of the Segura is left empty.

events.title: Carthage leads
events.text: After the battle of Alalia, Carthage leads the western Phoenicians, Gadir among them.

events.title: Greek wares spread
events.text: Greek pottery from Emporion reaches the villages of the Catalan coast.

events.title: Silver falls
events.text: Silver production at Rio Tinto declines sharply.

events.title: Cancho Roano
events.text: A palace-sanctuary rises in the Guadiana valley, heir to Tartessian traditions.

events.title: The silting estuary
events.text: The great estuary of the Guadalquivir slowly fills with silt, the future marshes of Doñana.

events.title: The Turdetani
events.text: Rich tombs and sanctuaries vanish from the lower valley; later writers call its people Turdetani.

events.title: Tartessos fades
events.text: Huelva's trade shrinks and Tartessos becomes a name in Greek books.

chartNote: Share of the area of modern Spain, by the world that dominated each present-day province. Regions are today's provinces; Phoenician colonies were small harbour enclaves on a native coast, and the boundaries of Tartessos are unknown. Dates are archaeological estimates, and the map is a simplification.
